readerTitle: Why the last few miles cost more than the first eight hundred
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (조립식 책상 제조사의 배송, 병원 예약 소프트웨어의 도입 지원) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 마지막 구간의 비용은 거리가 아니라 고객 한 명 한 명을 따로 상대해야 한다는 데서 나온다. 그래서 줄이는 방법도 '더 싸게 운반'이 아니라 '한 번에 더 많은 고객을 묶는 것'이다.
misconception: 배송비는 거리에 비례하니 멀리 옮기는 구간을 싸게 만들면 된다. 소프트웨어는 배송이 공짜이니 마지막 구간 문제가 없다.

sources.text: 물류·운영 관리의 표준 개념 (라스트 마일, 배송 밀도, 배송 실패)

factChecks.note: 책상 배송 계산: 장거리 트럭 $800 ÷ 400상자 = 상자당 $2. 밴 하루 $400 ÷ 20곳 = 정차당 $20. 합계 $2 + $3(창고) + $20 = $25, 이 중 마지막 구간 $20 = 80%. 같은 동네 묶음으로 하루 40곳이면 $400 ÷ 40 = $10.
소프트웨어 도입 지원 계산: 병원당 6시간 × 시간당 $50 = $300. 지역별 묶음 교육 예시는 수치 없이 원리만 서술했습니다.
업계에서 흔히 인용되는 '라스트 마일이 전체 배송비의 40~50%' 같은 수치는 출처마다 다르고 검증이 어려워 본문에 쓰지 않았습니다. 쓰려면 1차 출처를 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why the last few miles cost more than the first eight hundred
body: A furniture maker sends 400 flat-pack desks 800 km by truck to its city warehouse. The trip costs $800, or **$2 a desk**.
Then a van carries one desk the last 8 km to a customer's door. That short trip costs $20. The end of the journey is ten times pricier than the long part.

image.label: Long truck route on a map, then a tangle of short van routes at the end
image.brief: 지도 위에 공장에서 도시 창고까지 굵고 곧은 트럭 경로 하나, 창고에서 여러 집으로 뻗는 가늘고 구불구불한 밴 경로 수십 개. 앞 구간에 "$2 per desk", 끝 구간에 "$20 per desk" 라벨. 실제 기업 로고 없음.

cards.title: Delivery is eating your margin.
body: You run that furniture business. Delivery costs about $25 per desk, and customers expect it to be cheap.
Which move cuts the cost most?

options.text: Negotiate a cheaper truck contract from the factory to the warehouse
options.feedback: It feels like the big trip is the big cost. But that leg is only $2 a desk, so even a 25% cut saves 50 cents.

options.text: Deliver to each neighborhood on set days so vans make more stops per trip
options.feedback: You give up some speed and flexibility, but you attack the real cost: how many customers one van reaches in a day.

options.text: Offer free delivery everywhere to win more orders
options.feedback: More orders can help, but if they are scattered across the city, each van still drives far between stops. You'd pay more in total.

cards.title: Follow one desk.
body: The last leg is **80%** of the delivery cost. A van costs about $400 a day and reaches 20 homes. Fill the same day with 40 homes on nearby streets, and each stop drops to $10.

cards.title: The last mile
body: **The last mile** is the final step from the last shared point to each individual customer.

Before that point, many orders ride together and split the cost. After it, every customer is a separate stop, a separate wait and a separate chance that no one is home. So the cost depends less on distance than on **how many customers you reach per hour**.

image.label: Many boxes on one truck splitting into single boxes on separate paths
image.brief: 왼쪽: 상자 수십 개가 한 트럭에 실려 함께 이동("Shared"). 가운데 창고 아이콘에서 갈라져, 오른쪽: 상자 하나씩 각자 다른 집으로 가는 선("One at a time"). 갈라지는 지점을 강조.

cards.title: Software has a last mile too.
body: A company sells booking software to clinics. Sending the product to 1,000 clinics costs almost nothing. That's the shared part.
But each clinic needs its patient list imported, its calendar connected and its staff trained. That takes about 6 hours of a $50-an-hour specialist: **$300 per clinic**, one clinic at a time.
Same pattern as the desk. The bulk part scales. The step into each customer's hands does not.

image.label: One download arrow fanning out, then a person helping each clinic separately
image.brief: 왼쪽: 클라우드에서 여러 병원으로 동시에 뻗는 가는 화살표("Almost free"). 오른쪽: 병원마다 상담원 한 명이 앉아 데이터 옮기기와 교육을 돕는 장면("$300 each"). 실제 제품 로고 없음.

cards.title: Four ways to make the last mile cheaper.
body: Because the cost comes from handling customers one by one, the fixes all reduce that one-by-one work:
list: **Bunch customers:** delivery days by area, onboarding by cohort
**Move the handoff:** pickup points, lockers, self-serve setup guides
**Prevent repeats:** time windows, reminders, import templates that work the first time
**Price it honestly:** charge for fast or custom final steps
cards.callout: Cheaper trucks help a little. More customers per stop helps a lot.

cards.title: The last mile is also where customers judge you.
body: Pushing work onto customers saves money, but it shifts the cost to them. A missed delivery or a confusing setup is often the moment a customer decides you're not worth it.
Bunching also has a price: slower service. Some customers will pay more for speed or hand-holding. Cut the last mile where customers barely notice, and invest where they do.

cards.title: Back to the clinic software.
body: Onboarding costs $300 per clinic and sales are growing fast. Your team can't keep up, and new clinics wait weeks to start.

options.text: Stop onboarding help and send a video link instead
options.feedback: Cost drops to near zero, but clinics that never get set up never use the product. You save $300 and may lose the customer.

options.text: Build standard import templates and run weekly group training for new clinics
options.feedback: You bunch the one-by-one work and cut repeat fixes. Clinics wait a few days for a session, but each one costs far less to set up.

options.text: Keep onboarding as is and add a setup fee
options.feedback: The fee covers the cost, but the work still doesn't scale and the wait stays long. It can also slow sales.

cards.title: The costly part is reaching each customer, not moving the product.
body: Find the point where your shared work ends and one-by-one work begins. That's your last mile, and it usually holds the biggest savings.
**Try it today:** pick one recent order. List every step after it left the shared part of your business, and count how many were done for that customer alone.
